## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with liver cirrhosis based on statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. Most prominently, extracellular matrix organization (Reactome: R-HSA-1474244, p = 2.81 × 10−15, 50 associated proteins) and cell adhesion molecules (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes: 04514, p = 4.32 × 10−18, 40 associated proteins) strongly support the central role of fibrotic remodeling and altered tissue architecture in liver cirrhosis, consistent with extensive literature showing that excessive extracellular matrix deposition and dysregulated cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion are defining features of progressive hepatic scarring. In parallel, enrichment of actin-based cell projection (Gene Ontology: GO:0098858, p = 1.41 × 10−3, 15 associated proteins; supported by PMID:15661519) suggests cytoskeletal reorganization, which is relevant to activation of fibrogenic cells and structural changes in the cirrhotic liver.

Furthermore, neutrophil degranulation (Reactome: R-HSA-6798695, p = 1.22 × 10−16, 67 associated proteins), specific granule membrane (Gene Ontology: GO:0035579, p = 3.37 × 10−5, 14 associated proteins; supported by PMID:7334549), endopeptidase activity (Gene Ontology: GO:0004175, p = 1.03 × 10−8, 45 associated proteins), and zymogen activation (Gene Ontology: GO:0031638, p = 1.90 × 10−6, 11 associated proteins) collectively indicate a strong inflammatory and proteolytic signature. This is highly consistent with published evidence that chronic liver injury is accompanied by innate immune cell infiltration, release of granule enzymes, and protease-mediated matrix turnover, all of which contribute to hepatocellular damage and fibrosis progression. The enrichment of lysosome (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes: 04142, p = 4.31 × 10−11, 29 associated proteins) further supports altered degradative and autophagic pathways, which have been widely implicated in hepatocyte stress responses and stellate cell activation in cirrhosis.

In addition, carbohydrate derivative catabolic process (Gene Ontology: GO:1901136, p = 3.86 × 10−6, 24 associated proteins) and carbohydrate binding (Gene Ontology: GO:0030246, p = 2.99 × 10−10, 23 associated proteins) point to metabolic and glycan-interaction abnormalities, fitting with the profound metabolic dysfunction and altered glycoprotein handling known in advanced chronic liver disease. The enrichment of phenotype terms such as splenomegaly (Human Phenotype Ontology: HP:0001744, p = 7.52 × 10−3, 43 associated proteins) is also biologically plausible, as splenic enlargement is a classic consequence of portal hypertension in cirrhosis. Overall, these highly significant pathways converge on a coherent disease framework centered on extracellular matrix accumulation, inflammatory degranulation, protease activity, lysosomal dysfunction, and metabolic disturbance, all of which are well supported in the liver cirrhosis literature as key mechanisms driving disease progression and systemic complications.
